section: Why Not Just Use PubMed Alerts?
text:
Why Not Just Use PubMed Alerts?
PubMed alerts are a reasonable starting point, but they have a key limitation: they give you a flat, unsorted list. If you set up an alert for “inflammatory bowel disease,” every matching paper arrives in the same inbox pile - therapeutics next to epidemiology next to basic science - and you still have to read through everything to find what’s relevant to your work.
IBD LitMonitor takes a different approach. Instead of delivering a raw feed, it organizes papers into sub-fields so you can go straight to the topic area you care about and skip the rest. Each category is collapsible, so browsing the day’s literature takes minutes rather than a lengthy inbox triage.

Papers by Category






NoteHow to Read This Report



Coverage: PubMed queries across a broad set of IBD topic groups, deduplicated - each paper appears exactly once in the most specific matching category.
Categorisation: Automatic and imperfect - a paper found by multiple queries is assigned to the most specific one (e.g. a vedolizumab trial in children goes to Pediatric IBD). For keyword search across all categories or papers from the past 30 days, use the Interactive Dashboard.
Study design badges RCT Meta-analysis Review are shown only when PubMed has explicitly assigned a publication type. Papers published within the last 1-2 weeks often don’t have a badge yet.
★ Flagship journals: Papers from Gut, Gastroenterology, Lancet, NEJM, JCC, and other leading GI journals are marked ★.
Spotted something wrong or have a suggestion?  Send feedback →


Click a category to expand. Click a paper title to read its abstract.


Microbiome & Immunology  (17 papers)



Integrating complementary datasets for constructing microbiome-metabolome-disease pathways.  Bioinformatics (Oxford, England)  |  2026-10-20



Microbiome-metabolome-disease pathways play a central role in host health, but studying them is limited by the data available. Large clinical microbiome cohorts often lack metabolomic measurements, while multi-omics studies with paired profiles are typically small or incompletely phenotyped. Combining such complementary datasets is challenging: the metabolite is not measured in the clinical cohort, microbiome data are high-dimensional and compositional, and log-ratio analyses depend on an arbitrarily chosen reference taxon. We propose a framework that integrates a large target cohort that has microbiome and outcome data with a smaller external study that has paired microbiome-metabolome profiles. A high-dimensional structural equation model jointly links the microbiome, the metabolome and the disease outcome. It allows for unmeasured confounding and groups microbes into functional categories. We address compositionality with the additive log-ratio (ALR) transformation, estimate parameters by penalized two-stage least squares, and test metabolite-disease associations with a regularized permutation test. A novel multiple-reference procedure treats each microbe in turn as the ALR reference. It combines the resulting p-values with the Cauchy combination test and classifies microbes by stability selection, which makes inference robust to the choice of reference. In simulations, the method controls the type I error rate, and its power increases with both target and external sample sizes. An application to inflammatory bowel disease, integrating the FRAN and iHMP cohorts, reveals biologically interpretable microbiome-metabolome-disease links. The method is implemented in the R package MMDP, freely available at https://github.com/lei-fang-stat/MMDP. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.


Fang L, Ye C, Wang Y


DOI: 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag787  |  View on PubMed →





KCTD10 Modulates DSS-induced Ulcerative Colitis via Regulating Intestinal Stem Cell Function.  The American journal of pathology  |  2026-10-20



The incidence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) continues to rise annually, which severely threatens public health. While estimates indicate that current therapies cause a 30% IBD clinical treatment failure, the precise pathogenesis remains unclear. Here, we found that a key embryonic development regulator, KCTD10, is correlated with the severity of IBD. We observed enhanced KCTD10 expression during enterocolitis. Intestinal epithelial cell (IEC)-specific knockout of KCTD10 in mice impaired intestinal epithelial barrier function, activated intestinal adaptive immune response, and disrupted intestinal homeostasis. Furthermore, in a dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) -induced ulcerative colitis model, IEC deletion of KCTD10 exacerbated colonic inflammation and impaired post-injury repair. Mechanistically, KCTD10 deletion downregulated intestinal stem cell (ISC) marker genes and affected their function. Importantly, KCTD10 stabilizes the transcription factor ATOH1 by regulating its ubiquitination, thereby determining the fate of intestinal progenitor cells derived from Lgr5+ intestinal stem cells. Our data thus revealed a previously undescribed function of KCTD10 in modulating ulcerative colitis by regulating intestinal stem cell function.


Wang D, Xiao Y, Zhang J, Ding C, Li Z, Ren K


DOI: 10.1016/j.ajpath.2026.10.004  |  View on PubMed →





Crosstalk through cholinergic and aryl hydrocarbon receptor pathways in the anti-inflammatory actions of microbial metabolites.  Naunyn-Schmiedeberg’s archives of pharmacology  |  2026-10-20



The intestinal epithelium maintains immune and metabolic homeostasis at the host-microbiota interface, and its disruption contributes to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Microbial metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and indole derivatives are known to regulate epithelial and immune functions, but their roles in cholinergic signaling and aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) pathways remain incompletely understood. Caco-2 intestinal epithelial cells were stimulated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS; 10 µg/mL) and co-treated with SCFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate) or indole derivatives (IAA, IPA, IBA; 1000 µM). The AhR antagonist CH223191 was used to assess receptor involvement. Inflammatory markers (TNF-α, IL-6, COX-2), barrier integrity (FITC-dextran permeability, ZO-1 and occludin), cholinergic components (CHAT, ACHE, BCHE, α7nAChR, mAChR1, mAChR3), and AhR activation (nuclear localization, CYP1A1 expression) were analyzed using qPCR, ELISA, immunostaining, and enzymatic assays. Molecular docking was performed to predict metabolite-protein interactions. LPS induced inflammatory cytokine expression and barrier disruption, whereas SCFAs and indole derivatives significantly reduced inflammation, restored tight-junction organization, and decreased permeability. These metabolites enhanced CHAT and muscarinic receptor expression while suppressing ACHE upregulation, indicating restoration of cholinergic balance. Both groups reactivated AhR signaling, and AhR inhibition disrupted cholinergic regulation, supporting an AhR-dependent mechanism. Butyrate and indole-3-butyric acid exhibited the strongest protective effects. These findings identify a novel AhR-cholinergic axis in intestinal epithelial regulation and highlight microbial metabolites as promising therapeutic candidates for IBD.


Sonmez G, Sari S, Bodur E


DOI: 10.1007/s00210-026-06015-z  |  View on PubMed →





An engineered probiotic for diagnosis and mucosal healing in inflammatory bowel disease.★  Cell reports  |  2026-10-20



Early diagnosis and timely treatment of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) are critical to limit disease progression, yet integrated diagnostic-therapeutic strategies remain limited. Here, we design a synthetic probiotic system that responds to reactive oxygen species (ROS) to enable noninvasive detection of intestinal inflammation. We further engineer EcN-IL22, a therapeutic strain that conditionally expresses interleukin 22-fragment crystallizable (IL-22-Fc) fusion protein in situ to mitigate colitis-associated tissue damage. Mechanistically, EcN-IL22 activates epithelial IL-22 receptor 1/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (IL-22R1/STAT3) signaling, promoting epithelial barrier restoration and intestinal stem cell proliferation. We identify thyroid hormone receptor-interacting protein 13 (Trip13) and fidgetin-like 1 (Fignl1) as IL-22R1-responsive candidate genes associated with epithelial repair. Importantly, replacing the diagnostic output of the ROS-responsive circuit with IL-22-Fc enables inflammation-triggered therapeutic delivery and significantly alleviates colitis. Finally, EcN-IL22 demonstrates robust protective efficacy in a piglet colitis model, supporting its translational potential. Together, this work establishes an integrated probiotic platform for IBD diagnosis and regenerative therapy.


Zhao Y, Sun Y, Zhu X, Hu W, Chen S, Peng G, Yang S, Ma D, Mao X, Yi S


DOI: 10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118171  |  View on PubMed →





Gastrodin alleviates acute colitis with comorbid anxiety- and depression-like behaviours rather than cognitive dysfunction by modulating gut microbiota and suppressing inflammation.  Naunyn-Schmiedeberg’s archives of pharmacology  |  2026-10-19



Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients frequently suffer from emotional disturbances, predominantly anxiety- and depression-like symptoms, and may also have cognitive dysfunction, but the mechanisms remain unclear, and no therapies targeting the gut or nervous system exist. Gastrodin (GAS), the primary active component of Gastrodia elata, has anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects. Whether GAS can alleviate acute colitis with comorbid anxiety- and depression-like behaviours or cognitive dysfunction via the gut-brain axis is unknown. Using a 3% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model, we administered GAS (240 mg/kg) by gavage for 7 days. The open field, elevated plus maze, tail suspension, and forced swimming tests showed that GAS improved behavioural abnormalities (including anxiety- and depression-like behaviours); it also restored colon length and reduced colonic histopathological injury. Metagenomic sequencing revealed that GAS reshaped the gut microbiota, increasing Sporosarcina and Nitrospirae while decreasing Clostridiaceae and Lachnospiraceae. Untargeted metabolomics indicated that GAS shifted the metabolic profile away from DSS and normalized taurine levels, and KEGG pathway analysis suggested that GAS may partially ameliorate DSS-induced metabolic disturbances by downregulating virulence-related pathways and upregulating energy metabolic pathways such as the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation relative to DSS. Western blot confirmed that GAS restored the tight junction protein Occludin and decreased TNF-α. Quantitative proteomics demonstrated that GAS reversed the aberrant expression of 191 colonic proteins. These results demonstrate correlative associations between GAS treatment and the alleviation of acute colitis and behavioural abnormalities, alongside concurrent changes in gut microbiota composition, metabolite profiles, and intestinal barrier proteins. Whether these associations reflect a causal gut-brain axis mechanism requires direct experimental validation. GAS modulates the microbiota, partially restores metabolism, repairs the gut barrier, and suppresses local inflammation, suggesting a potential gut-brain axis mechanism. These findings position GAS as a promising candidate for further mechanistic and translational investigation in IBD-associated behavioural comorbidities.


Song JL, Wu RC, Sun R, Gao YX, He BQ, Xie YJ, Xie JS, Li XR, Tong FX, Liu Y


DOI: 10.1007/s00210-026-05930-5  |  View on PubMed →





Reviewing preclinical evidence for potent anti-colitogenic effects of the “bee glue” propolis.Review  European journal of microbiology & immunology  |  2026-10-19



The incidence and disease burden of inflammatory bowel diseases including ulcerative colitis have risen significantly in recent years, and current treatment remains limited by adverse effects and insufficient long-term efficacy, creating demand for alternative or adjunct treatment options. The “bee glue” propolis, a natural compound with a long history of medicinal use, has attracted growing attention for its anti-oxidant, anti-inflammatory, and immune-modulatory properties. This review summarizes and critically evaluates research into anti-colitogenic effects of propolis and its bioactive molecules in experimental colitis animal models. Our structured literature search revealed 21 preclinical studies showing that application of propolis and derivatives resulted in clinical and histopathological improvement of colitis. Treated animals presented with reduced colonic inflammation, restored intestinal barrier integrity, and a more diverse commensal gut microbiota. Notably, the composition of propolis varied considerably between studies depending on geographical and botanical origins and extraction method of the compound, for instance. In conclusion, propolis and derivatives exert potent anti-colitogenic effects in vivo, and might constitute promising disease-alleviating treatment options in human intestinal inflammation, including ulcerative colitis that should be further unravelled in future clinical trials.


Quincke SM, Bereswill S, Heimesaat MM


DOI: 10.1556/1886.2026.00051  |  View on PubMed →





Monocyte surface Y RNAs potentiate innate immunity.  Nature cell biology  |  2026-10-19



RNAs can associate with the surface of diverse cell types, yet the functions of specific RNA species on primary immune cells remain unclear. Here, utilizing methods developed to profile, image and quantify surface RNAs in rare primary cell populations, we found that Y RNAs, a family of small noncoding RNAs, preferentially localize to human monocyte surface. In an exploratory pooled inflammatory bowel disease cohort, the proportion of cell-surface-Y-RNA-positive peripheral monocytes was markedly higher in patients with inflammatory bowel disease than in healthy donors or individuals with irritable bowel syndrome. In vivo depletion of cell-surface Y RNAs ameliorates disease activity in mice with colitis. Mechanistically, cell-surface Y RNAs co-cluster with Toll-like receptors TLR2 and TLR4, bind extracellular histones and promote receptor-mediated histone recognition, thereby activating NF-κB and AP-1 signalling and increasing IL6 expression and IL-6 secretion. These findings identify cell-surface Y RNAs as previously unrecognized amplifiers of inflammatory activation.


Jiang X, He W, Xu C, Zheng W, Li C, Xu D, Shao Q, Li Y, Liu Z, Li W


DOI: 10.1038/s41556-026-02100-w  |  View on PubMed →





Myrica rubra juice attenuates DSS-induced colitis and is associated with changes in the gut microbiota-metabolite-host axis.  Food & function  |  2026-10-19



Ulcerative colitis (UC) is characterized by chronic intestinal inflammation and impaired mucosal barrier function. Myrica rubra contains polyphenols and flavonoids, but the mechanisms underlying its potential protective effects in colitis remain unclear. We evaluated Myrica rubra juice (MRJ) in a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model of colitis and a TNF-α-injured colonic organoid model. The study combined 16S rRNA gene sequencing, untargeted serum and fecal metabolomics, and molecular docking. MRJ treatment attenuated disease severity and was associated with increased expression of occludin and MUC2 in DSS-treated mice. MRJ also altered microbial diversity and taxonomic composition in a taxon-specific manner. Serum and fecal metabolomic profiles differed after MRJ treatment, including pathways related to amino acid and bile acid metabolism. Integrated analyses identified associations among microbial taxa, putatively annotated metabolites, and host inflammatory and barrier-related variables. Direct exposure to 20% (v/v) whole MRJ increased occludin immunofluorescence in TNF-α-injured colonic organoids cultured without a gut microbial community. This single-marker result is consistent with an epithelial response to whole MRJ under the applied in vitro conditions. Molecular docking generated predicted poses and docking scores for selected parent compound-protein pairs. These calculations did not demonstrate physical binding, functional inhibition, or target engagement in vivo. Together, the findings support a direct epithelial response and identify concurrent microbiota-associated changes. However, the present design could not determine whether these microbial changes contributed to protection. It also could not separate or quantify the host-directed and microbiota-mediated contributions or identify the active chemical species.


Chen L, Ye Y, Ma Y, Cheng D, Cheng Y, Guo Y, Liu C, Qian H


DOI: 10.1039/d6fo01741j  |  View on PubMed →





Primetime for the Gasdermins Seesaw in Intestinal Homeostasis and Digestive Disorders.Review  Medicinal research reviews  |  2026-10-18



The five pore-forming gasdermins (GSDMs, namely GSDMA-E) are best known for executing pyroptosis, a lytic and highly inflammatory form of programmed cell death. Accumulating evidence over the past decade has unveiled diverse nonlytic functions of GSDMs in digestive homeostasis and disease. GSDMs preserve intestinal barrier integrity and mucosal immunity under physiological conditions, whereas their dysregulated activation fuels tissue injury across a spectrum of digestive diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease, acute intestinal injury, radiation enteritis, acute pancreatitis, and liver disorders. Notably, the functional outcome of GSDM activation is highly context-dependent: the same protein can be either protective or injurious. This duality extends to digestive oncology, where GSDM-mediated pyroptosis can stimulate or suppress antitumor immunity. GSDM-targeted drugs, including GSDMD agonists, GSDMD inhibitors, and GSDME inhibitors, have shown encouraging efficacy in preclinical models, although none have yet reached the clinic. Here, we review the dual roles of GSDMs across the digestive system, outline the mechanistic basis of their form-, cell-, and tissue-specific functions, and discuss the progress and remaining challenges in GSDM-targeted therapy.


Liu Q, Liu H, Liu Y, Wang C


DOI: 10.1002/med.70114  |  View on PubMed →





2’-Fucosyllactose enhances indole-3-lactic acid production by Bifidobacterium bifidum DNG-08 and alleviates colitis-associated bone loss: Associations with microbiota remodeling and intestinal AHR-related responses.  Microbiological research  |  2026-10-17



Inflammatory bowel disease is frequently associated with an imbalance in bone remodeling and a decline in bone mass, however, there is a lack of systematic research on microbiome-based intervention strategies targeting colitis-associated bone loss. In this study, Bifidobacterium bifidum DNG-08 (DNG-08) was selected from four candidate strains based on its favorable 2’-fucosyllactose (2’-FL) utilization and indole-3-lactic acid (ILA) production. Genomic annotation revealed that DNG-08 harbors functional genes related to fucosylated oligosaccharide utilization and the conversion of tryptophan to ILA. In a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model, combined intervention with DNG-08 and 2’-FL significantly alleviated colitis-associated phenotypes, and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels by 13.33%-58.69%, while increasing IL-10-1.23 times that of the DSS group. Simultaneously, the combined intervention improved trabecular bone microstructure, increasing the bone formation marker procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (PINP) by 14.61%-56.37%, decreasing the bone resorption marker C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX-I) by 17.03%-21.77%, and upregulating the expression of Wnt3a, β-catenin, and Runx2. Gut microbiota analysis showed that combined intervention could partially reverse DSS-induced dysbiosis, enriching potentially beneficial bacterial taxa while reducing inflammation-associated genera. Notably, combined treatment group exhibited elevated serum ILA levels, increased colonic aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) fluorescence, and upregulatied CYP1A1 expression. Correlation analysis identified significant associations among serum ILA, AHR-related indicators, selected bacterial genera, and bone remodeling parameters. This study highlights that strain-substrate matching may serve as a precise synbiotic strategy to improve inflammation-related gut-bone axis dysfunction.


Wang X, Zheng B, Sun Y, Liu L, Li C


DOI: 10.1016/j.micres.2026.128781  |  View on PubMed →





Fecal Microbiota Transfer for Recurrent Clostridioides difficile Infection: A Retrospective Single-Center Analysis.  Zeitschrift fur Gastroenterologie  |  2026-10-16



Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is the leading cause of healthcare-associated infectious diarrhea. Despite high initial response rates to antibiotic therapy, recurrence occurs in approximately 20% of patients. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) has emerged as an effective treatment option for multiple recurrences, demonstrating high efficacy and a favorable safety profile. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of FMT in patients with recurrent CDI (rCDI). In this single-center retrospective study, 75 patients who underwent FMT for rCDI between November 2016 and January 2026 after experiencing at least two recurrences despite standard antibiotic therapy were included. Donor screening was performed according to the requirements of the German Federal Institute for Drugs and Medical Devices (BfArM). Following CDI-directed antibiotic pretreatment, FMT was administered either by colonoscopy, oral capsules, or a combination of both. Patients were followed for three months. The primary endpoint was the absence of diarrhea as a surrogate marker for rCDI, including a predefined subgroup analysis of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Follow-up data were available for 65 patients, of whom 56 (86.1%) achieved sustained clinical remission. Patients with concomitant IBD (n=15) showed a comparable response rate (86.7%). The route of FMT administration had no significant impact on treatment outcome. Overall, FMT was well tolerated, with only four patients (5.3%) reporting predominantly self-limiting adverse events. FMT is a highly effective and safe treatment for recurrent CDI, including in multimorbid patients and those with concomitant IBD. Die Clostridioides-difficile-Infektion (CDI) ist die häufigste Ursache einer nosokomial erworbenen infektiösen Diarrhoe. Trotz guter Ansprechraten unter antibiotischer Therapie treten Rezidive bei ca. 20% der Patienten auf. Der fäkale Mikrobiotatransfer (FMT) ist insbesondere bei multiplen Rezidiven eine effektive Therapieoption mit hoher Wirksamkeit und gutem Sicherheitsprofil. Ziel dieser Studie war die Untersuchung von Effektivität und Sicherheit des FMT bei rezidivierender CDI (rCDI).In einer monozentrischen retrospektiven Analyse wurden 75 Patienten untersucht, die zwischen November 2016 und Januar 2026 nach mindestens zwei Rezidiven einer CDI mittels FMT behandelt wurden. Das Spenderscreening erfolgte gemäß BfArM-Vorgaben. Nach vorbereitender antibiotischer Therapie wurde der FMT kolonoskopisch, oral mittels Kapseln oder kombiniert appliziert. Die Nachbeobachtung betrug drei Monate. Primärer Endpunkt war das Ausbleiben einer Diarrhoe als Surrogatmarker für eine rCDI, einschließlich einer Subgruppenanalyse bei chronisch entzündlichen Darmerkrankungen (CED).Von 65 Patienten mit vollständiger Nachbeobachtung erreichten 56 (86,1 %) eine anhaltende Symptomfreiheit. Auch Patienten mit CED (n=15) zeigten vergleichbare Ansprechraten (86,7 %). Die Applikationsform beeinflusste den Therapieerfolg nicht. Der FMT war insgesamt sehr gut verträglich; lediglich vier Patienten (5.3 %) berichteten über überwiegend selbstlimitierende Nebenwirkungen.Der FMT ist eine hochwirksame und sichere Therapie der rCDI, auch bei multimorbiden Patienten und Patienten mit CED.

Abstract not available.

Microbiome-Endocannabinoidome Crosstalk as an Immunometabolic Rheostat in Inflammatory Disease.Review  FASEB bioAdvances  |  2026-10-15



Chronic inflammatory diseases reflect disrupted coordination among microbial ecology, epithelial barriers, lipid signaling, and immunity. The microbiome-endocannabinoidome (eCBome) axis is already recognized as a regulator of metabolism, permeability, and inflammatory tone; the unresolved issue is how to distinguish direct crosstalk from parallel or associative changes. This review therefore operationalizes the axis as an immunometabolic rheostat defined by five measurable domains: microbial functions and metabolites, compartment-specific eCBome ligands and enzymes, barrier integrity and microbial translocation, immune-cell programming, and tissue or clinical outcomes. We distinguish classical endocannabinoids (anandamide and 2-arachidonoylglycerol) from the endocannabinoid-related N-acylethanolamines palmitoylethanolamide and oleoylethanolamide, which act prominently through PPARα, TRPV1, GPR119, and related pathways. The encapsulation efficiency of phycocyanin peptide nanoparticles (PCP-NPs) reached 91.33%, with markedly enhanced gastrointestinal stability and bioavailability. In mouse experiments, PCP-NPs reduced the disease activity index of ulcerative colitis mice, repaired colonic injury, down-regulated pro-inflammatory cytokines, and up-regulated anti-inflammatory cytokines and intestinal tight junction proteins. Three core anti-inflammatory peptides, YAINA, FPYTT, and YVTYA, were isolated and identified. Pitfalls in the Diagnosis and Classification of Crohn’s Disease: Misdiagnosis, Overdiagnosis, and Misclassification.Review  The Turkish journal of gastroenterology : the official journal of Turkish Society of Gastroenterology  |  2026-10-06



Crohn’s disease (CD) remains challenging to diagnose and classify accurately despite advances in endoscopy, cross-sectional imaging, intestinal ultrasound, and inflammatory biomarkers. Earlier diagnosis and treat-to-target strategies have improved outcomes but have also increased the risk of misdiagnosis, overdiagnosis, and misclassification of disease activity or severity. Misdiagnosis may expose patients without CD to unnecessary immunosuppressive therapy while delaying recognition and treatment of the true underlying condition, including drug-induced enteropathy, bile acid malabsorption, irritable bowel syndrome, and other disorders of gut-brain interaction. This is particularly relevant in tuberculosis (TB)-endemic regions, where intestinal TB remains one of the most challenging mimics of CD. Overdiagnosis commonly results from overinterpretation of nonspecific symptoms, incidental terminal ileitis, or isolated endoscopic and histological abnormalities. Elevated fecal calprotectin lacks specificity, whereas a low value provides stronger evidence against CD, although it does not reliably exclude isolated small-bowel disease. Misclassification most often reflects underestimation of disease severity, particularly when standard ileocolonoscopy fails to detect proximal small bowel or transmural disease or when discordant endoscopic and cross-sectional imaging findings are not appropriately reconciled. This review examines the major diagnostic and classification pitfalls in CD and proposes a practical, multidisciplinary approach based on integrating complementary investigations, longitudinal reassessment, and diagnostic reconsideration when uncertainty persists.

Early case reports and observational studies have suggested an association between isotretinoin and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). However, large cohort studies and meta-analyses have not demonstrated a meaningful association between isotretinoin use and IBD development. Most prior research has focused on incident IBD risk, with limited attention to disease activity among patients with established IBD. We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of patients with Crohn’s disease (CD) or ulcerative colitis (UC) treated with isotretinoin between 2015 and 2025. Inclusion required at least 1 IBD assessment within the 4 months before and 12 months after isotretinoin initiation. Disease activity was assessed using Harvey-Bradshaw Index (HBI), partial Mayo score (pMS), inflammatory biomarkers, and in some patients, intestinal ultrasound and fecal calprotectin. The primary outcome was composite IBD status change, defined as new clinical activity (Δ ≥ 1 in HBI/pMS), or isotretinoin discontinuation attributed to IBD activity. Thirty-seven patients met inclusion criteria (57% CD, 43% UC). Most patients were in clinical remission at baseline (86%). Following isotretinoin exposure, 92% remained in remission, with no significant changes in HBI, pMS, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, or fecal calprotectin. IBD status change occurred in 4 patients (11%), with events largely attributable to underlying IBD-related factors, including biologic transitions, anti-drug antibody development, or medication dose adjustments. Beyond the pelvis: redefining endometriosis as a systemic inflammatory disorder. A systematic review and meta-analysis.Review  Autoimmunity reviews  |  2026-10-20



Endometriosis has traditionally been defined as a disease localized to the pelvis. However, its clinical presentation is often accompanied by systemic comorbidities that extend far beyond the pelvic cavity, a phenomenon that challenges the traditional disease paradigm. This study aimed to comprehensively assess the associations between endometriosis and autoimmune diseases, allergic conditions, chronic pain syndromes, and endocrine disorders through a systematic review and meta-analysis, thereby providing evidence for redefining endometriosis as a systemic immuno-inflammatory disorder. To conduct this study, a comprehensive search strategy was employed to identify relevant published studies. Electronic databases, including Web of Science and Medline, were searched from their inception up to December 31, 2025. We additionally examined the reference lists of all identified papers to capture any additional articles that were not identified through the electronic database searches. Eligible studies were observational in design (cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional) and reported quantitative data on the association between endometriosis and predefined comorbidities in women. Exclusion criteria included non-human studies, non-English publications, secondary literature types (e.g., reviews, case reports), and studies lacking sufficient data for effect size calculation. Quality assessment was conducted based on the GRADE criteria. The final analysis included 55 studies that met the predefined inclusion criteria and were incorporated into the comprehensive analysis. Of these, 48 studies provided sufficient data for quantitative synthesis (meta-analysis). Specifically, 32 studies investigated the association between endometriosis and autoimmune diseases: 14 on systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), 8 on Sjögren’s syndrome (SS), 10 on rheumatoid arthritis (RA), 5 on multiple sclerosis (MS), 5 on celiac disease (CLD), and 4 on inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Additionally, 17 studies examined associations with allergic diseases, 13 focused on pain syndromes, and 6 explored associations with endocrine disorders. Meta-analysis showed that women with endometriosis had a significantly higher risk of certain autoimmune diseases in cohort studies, including SLE (RR: 1.81, 95% CI: 1.50-2.18), SS (RR: 1.54, 95% CI: 1.40-1.71), and RA (RR: 1.71, 95% CI: 1.40-2.09), as well as significantly higher odds in case-control and cross-sectional studies for SLE (OR: 3.93, 95% CI: 2.59-5.98), SS (OR: 3.13, 95% CI: 1.10-8.90), RA (OR: 2.27, 95% CI: 1.75-2.95), MS (OR: 2.30, 95% CI: 1.57-3.37), CLD (OR: 4.50, 95% CI: 1.94-10.42), and IBD (OR: 2.82, 95% CI: 0.58-13.61). Significant associations were also observed for allergic conditions-such as asthma (RR: 1.27, 95% CI: 1.14-1.40) and eczema (OR: 1.58, 95% CI: 1.34-1.87)-and for pain syndromes including fibromyalgia (RR: 1.65, 95% CI: 1.42-1.92), chronic fatigue syndrome (RR: 1.41, 95% CI: 1.31-1.51), and irritable bowel syndrome (RR: 2.51, 95% CI: 1.55-4.07; OR: 3.49, 95% CI: 3.21-3.80). The associations with various comorbidities are underpinned by shared mechanisms of immune dysregulation and central sensitization. This paradigm shift necessitates a move in clinical practice from a purely gynecological intervention model toward a patient-centered, comprehensive multidisciplinary management approach. It also provides a theoretical foundation for developing novel treatment strategies targeting shared pathological pathways. CRD420251258716.

IgG is the most abundant antibody in the human circulation. It carries a single conserved glycosylation site, Asparagine 297, in its Fc domain. This N-glycan is critical for the ability of the antibody to activate immune cells via binding to, and cross-linking Fc receptors in order to elicit functional responses. First documented in the context of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), the IgG N-glycan may undergo changes that are correlated to host health. We present a narrative in-depth comparison of changes incurred by IgG N-glycans in autoimmune diseases; RA, systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, type I diabetes, primary biliary cholangitis and inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis). Based on a systematic literature search, we identify common traits and features that are specific for any one autoimmune disease. Our analysis shows that the single most common trend in most of the conditions analyzed here is increased IgG agalactosylation. Changes to the IgG N-glycan typically accompany and often precede disease onset and flare-ups, while they decrease in remission and pregnancy. The correlation of agalactosylated IgG with inflammatory disease is so striking that the agalactosylated IgG N-glycan has long been viewed as inflammatory and even pathogenic. Yet, despite the association with inflammation, any mechanism by which disease-associated IgG N-glycans may mediate their pro-inflammatory nature remains enigmatic.

ObjectiveInterleukin-23 (IL-23) inhibitors are widely used for psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease, yet their long-term safety profiles require continual monitoring. This retrospective observational real-world study aimed to detect potential disproportionate reporting signals associated with tildrakizumab, risankizumab, and guselkumab using the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS).MethodsAE reports for tildrakizumab, risankizumab, and guselkumab from Q3 2017 to Q3 2025 were retrieved from FAERS. Disproportionality analysis using reporting odds ratios (RORs) was performed, and reported adverse events were classified by system organ classes (SOCs).ResultsA total of 1124, 8574, and 14597 AEs were retrieved for the three IL-23 inhibitors, generating 42, 286, and 348 disproportionate reporting signals, and accumulating 23, 24, and 24 SOCs. Frequently reported AEs included drug ineffectiveness, psoriasis, injection-site reactions, and infections. Disproportionate reporting signals not listed in the current FDA-approved product label comprised cardiovascular events (e.g., myocardial infarction; tildrakizumab ROR = 6.45), malignancies (e.g., malignant melanoma; risankizumab ROR = 8.57), hepatobiliary disorders, and renal complications.ConclusionThese exploratory, hypothesis-generating disproportionate reporting signals may inform routine pharmacovigilance practice for IL-23 inhibitors, alongside well-established common reported events such as infections and systemic reactions. Further pharmacoepidemiologic studies are needed to validate these observations.

Updated treatment targets in inflammatory bowel disease (STRIDE-III): an initiative of the International Organization for the Study of IBD.Review★  The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology  |  2026-10-19



Since Selecting Therapeutic Targets in Inflammatory Bowel Disease-II (STRIDE-II), new evidence has become available across inflammatory and patient-centred outcomes. We aimed to update the STRIDE recommendations for Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL for studies published after the STRIDE-II search period. Findings were integrated with surveys of International Organization for the Study of IBD (IOIBD) members and paediatric gastroenterologists from the Porto group of the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition. Statements were subsequently voted on using a modified Delphi approach; consensus was defined as ≥75% of participants rating a statement 7-10 on a 10-point scale. Of 13 071 records identified in the systematic review, 1018 were included. Surveys were completed by 60 of 79 IOIBD gastroenterologists and 23 of 30 paediatric gastroenterologists in the Porto group. STRIDE-III defines three conceptually distinct categories of treatment targets. Actionable targets include clinical response and remission, which reflect patient priorities, and objective inflammatory targets (C-reactive protein normalisation, faecal calprotectin within target range, and endoscopic remission), supported by interventional evidence demonstrating benefits of target-guided treatment modification. Adjunctive targets (ie, urgency, histological remission in ulcerative colitis, transmural remission in Crohn’s disease, and growth) are supported by studies showing association with favourable outcomes and guide treatment optimisation and tighter monitoring but do not necessarily require a change in therapeutic class. Patient-centred targets (ie, disability, fatigue, and quality of life) directly reflect patients’ well-being and are impaired in a substantial proportion of patients with inflammatory bowel disease; impairment should prompt assessment of inflammation and alternative causes and management through shared decision-making. Targets are further classified as immediate, short-term, intermediate, and long-term. STRIDE-III also defines treatment-specific times to target achievement, new faecal calprotectin thresholds, and adaptations for resource-limited settings. STRIDE-III distinguishes targets that should prompt treatment change from those that primarily guide optimisation and monitoring, while establishing a separate patient-centred pathway based on shared decision-making. This framework supports consistent, evidence-based treat-to-target care.
